attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Fair paraphrase of the present-state complaint. The 'different product' clause is evaluative rhetoric with no test attached.

contract.note: Reading 'know it'll do it' as relying on it without checking, and capability clarity as users being able to predict success, is an ordinary reading. The 2025 window is an inference but reasonable.

evidence.note: Dated OpenAI disclosure of deep research failures and poor uncertainty calibration. Partial support only: it covers one feature and is a company statement, not a representative evaluation.
Launch documentation describing what o3 can do with images. It does not show whether users understood when tasks would succeed.

reviews.rationale: e1 gives partial support for unreliable execution in one feature. Nothing in the packet is a representative evaluation of ordinary ChatGPT requests, and there is no user study on whether capability limits were clear. The 'different product' clause cannot be tested. The contract's support condition is not met and the evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition matches the sentence. However, the claim record still lists 'hundreds of billions' as original_threshold, even though the revision says that figure was removed.

contract.note: The contract brings back the 'hundreds of billions' threshold (≥$200B) that the claim revision removed as belonging to a neighbouring sentence. It also requires generative-AI-only spending on a consistent accounting basis. That is a stricter reading than the plain words, which only say 'incredible amounts of capital'.

evidence.note: Stargate announcement: a stated $500B plan with Microsoft and Nvidia as technology partners. It is an intention, not secured or spent capital.
Microsoft's capex for the quarter, mixing cloud and AI spending. It is not a figure for generative-AI infrastructure alone.
Alphabet's planned company-wide capex of about $75B for 2025. No generative-AI allocation is broken out.
AP report giving Microsoft and Nvidia market values above $2T. Market value does not measure investment.

reviews.rationale: The contract adds a threshold the drafter removed, so it is unfair to the speaker's words. Even on its own terms, the packet gives no comparable, non-overlapping total of capital for generative-AI infrastructure. The available figures are plans or mixed cloud/AI capex. The large scale of AI-directed spending is plausible, but these records do not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Faithful. 'Cultists' is fairly rendered as ardent supporters. The 'famous for' clause is a claim about comparative reputation.

contract.note: Reading the warning as advice to verify output is fair. Asking for evidence that inconsistency outweighed efficacy in reputation follows the comparative wording.

evidence.note: Willison, an enthusiastic user, writes in March 2025 that you must test what LLMs write. This supports the advocate-warning clause only; it says nothing on public reputation.

reviews.rationale: The advocate-warning clause is supported by e1. The main claim, that LLMs were known more for inconsistency than for efficacy, has no representative reputation evidence in the packet, and the relevant survey sources were inaccessible or outside the window. One part is supported and the other is unsettled, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Faithful. The 'iPhone moment' part is an analogy with no observable endpoint. The 'no one thing they do well' part is a firm, categorical claim that can be tested.

contract.note: The categorical reading (not even one task done competently) is the ordinary meaning of 'any one thing they do well', and the contract does not require perfection. The iPhone part is rightly treated as not testable.

evidence.note: Independent METR measurement, March 2025: models beat experts on most exam-style problems and succeed almost every time on short tasks. That is competent performance on bounded tasks.
Anthropic's own disclosure of 63.7% on SWE-bench Verified, with its method stated. It corroborates bounded coding competence; it is a vendor result.
OpenAI's hallucination rates show factual unreliability. That does not show poor performance on every task.

reviews.rationale: An independent evaluation from the period (e1) shows LLMs performing competently on bounded task classes, and a vendor result (e2) corroborates it. This meets the contract's contradiction condition for the categorical claim. The hallucination data qualifies reliability but does not rescue 'no one thing'. The 'iPhone moment' part cannot be scored.
